notions.question: What economic policy did Margaret Thatcher set against the Keynesian consensus?
notions.definition: Inspired by the economists Milton Friedman and Friedrich Hayek, Margaret Thatcher (Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990) made the fight against inflation her priority, at the expense of full employment. Monetarism means controlling the growth of the money supply (Medium-Term Financial Strategy, 1980), reducing the budget deficit and keeping interest rates high. The policy went hand in hand with "rolling back the frontiers of the state": cuts in income tax, deregulation, privatisation, curbs on trade union power. In the short term, the 1980-1981 recession pushed unemployment above three million and hit Northern industry hard; inflation fell markedly in the mid-1980s. Strict monetarism was gradually relaxed.

items: Priority: price stability, control of the money supply
Cuts in public spending and in the deficit
"There is no alternative" (TINA): refusal to return to reflationary policies

termes.definition: A doctrine giving priority to controlling the money supply in order to fight inflation.
The amount of money in circulation.
The decline of industry within the economy.

exemple.texte: The phrase "The lady's not for turning" (1980 Conservative Party conference) can be discussed as a refusal to make an economic U-turn despite rising unemployment.

confusions.explication: The former targets inflation through money; the latter targets full employment through demand.

verification: What were the immediate social consequences of monetarism?

notions.question: Why and how did Thatcher privatise the major public corporations?
notions.definition: The Thatcher governments sold most of the nationalised industries to the private sector: British Telecom (1984), British Gas (1986, with the "Tell Sid" advertising campaign), British Airways and Rolls-Royce (1987), British Steel (1988), the water companies (1989), electricity (1990-1991). Aims: efficiency through competition and profit, revenue for the state, reduced trade union influence, and the creation of a "popular capitalism" through individual share ownership. The right of council tenants to buy their homes (Right to Buy, Housing Act 1980) followed the same logic of a "property-owning democracy". The record is debated: efficiency gains in some sectors, but concentration of share ownership, price rises and private monopolies requiring regulators.

termes.definition: The sale of a public corporation to the private sector.
The spread of share ownership across the population.
The option for tenants to buy their home.

exemple.texte: An "If you see Sid, tell him" advertisement (British Gas, 1986) can be analysed as a tool for promoting popular share ownership.

confusions.explication: Privatisation changes the owner; deregulation loosens the rules.

verification: What were the political aims of privatisation?

notions.titre: The trade unions and the miners' strike
notions.question: How did Thatcher reduce the power of the trade unions?
notions.definition: Seeing union power as a cause of decline and of the crises of the 1970s, the Thatcher governments curbed it through successive laws: the Employment Acts of 1980 and 1982 (limits on picketing, secondary action and the closed shop) and the Trade Union Act 1984 (compulsory secret ballot before a strike). The decisive conflict was the miners' strike (March 1984 - March 1985), led by Arthur Scargill's National Union of Mineworkers against the closure of pits deemed uneconomic by the National Coal Board. Called without a national ballot and marked by violent clashes (Orgreave, June 1984), it ended in defeat for the miners. Union membership and the number of strike days then fell lastingly.

lignes: Employment Acts: picketing, secondary action, closed shop
Trade Union Act: secret ballot before a strike

termes.definition: A group of strikers outside the workplace.
The requirement to be a union member in order to be hired.

exemple.texte: A photograph of miners facing mounted police in 1984 can be discussed as a symbol of the confrontation between the government and working-class trade unionism.

verification: Why is the 1984-1985 miners' strike a turning point?

notions.titre: The Big Bang in the City (1986)
notions.question: How did the City of London become a leading global financial centre?
notions.definition: The "Big Bang" refers to the sudden deregulation of the London Stock Exchange on 27 October 1986: abolition of fixed commissions, end of the separation between brokers and market makers (jobbers), opening of stockbroking firms' capital to banks, including foreign ones, and the switch to electronic trading. Prepared by the abolition of exchange controls (1979), the reform attracted the major international banks and made the City one of the world's leading financial centres. It contributed to the growth of financial services, but also to the financialisation of the economy, to regional inequalities and to risk-taking that was criticised after the 2008 crisis.

items: 27 October 1986: Big Bang (negotiable commissions, end of the broker / jobber separation, foreign banks admitted, electronic trading)
Consequences: boom in the City, takeovers of British firms by foreign banks, "yuppie" culture
Debates: weight of finance, gap between London and the former industrial regions

termes.definition: Removing or loosening the rules governing a sector.
A city where financial activities are concentrated.

exemple.texte: A 1986 press article describing trading floors deserted in favour of screens illustrates the switch to electronic trading.

confusions.explication: Two different strands of Thatcherite liberalisation.

verification: Which measures made up the 1986 Big Bang?

notions.titre: The poll tax and Thatcher's downfall
notions.question: Why did Margaret Thatcher leave office in 1990?
notions.definition: The "poll tax" (officially the Community Charge) replaced local taxes based on the value of homes with a flat-rate charge per adult, regardless of income. Introduced in Scotland in 1989 and then in England and Wales in April 1990, it was seen as deeply unfair and provoked widespread non-payment and violent demonstrations (London, 31 March 1990). Divisions over Europe added to this: the resignation of Deputy Prime Minister Geoffrey Howe and his resignation speech (November 1990) triggered Michael Heseltine's challenge for the party leadership. With insufficient support in the first round, Thatcher withdrew and resigned at the end of November 1990; John Major succeeded her. The poll tax was replaced by the council tax (1993).

lignes: Poll tax in England and Wales
Geoffrey Howe's resignation and speech; Heseltine's challenge; Thatcher withdraws

termes.definition: A tax that funds local authorities.

exemple.texte: A 1990 cartoon showing Thatcher surrounded by ministers brandishing knives can be discussed in connection with the Conservative Party revolt.

confusions.explication: Thatcher did not lose a general election: she was removed by her own party.

choix.explication: Negotiable commissions, foreign banks, electronic trading.

choix.explication: She was forced out by her party in 1990.

flashcards.question: Outline Thatcherism: economic policy, privatisation, trade unions, the City, downfall.
flashcards.reponse: Monetarism (Friedman, Hayek): priority to inflation, money supply, high interest rates, spending cuts; 1980-1981 recession, more than 3 million unemployed; TINA. Privatisation: BT (1984), British Gas (1986), BA (1987), water (1989), electricity (1990-1991); Right to Buy (1980); popular capitalism. Trade unions: Employment Acts 1980, 1982, Trade Union Act 1984; miners' strike 1984-1985 (Scargill) lost. Big Bang (27 October 1986): deregulation of the City. Downfall: poll tax (1989-1990), divisions over Europe, Howe's resignation, Heseltine's challenge, departure in November 1990; succeeded by Major.
erreurs: Saying that Thatcher lost an election
